title: 2 Chronicles 18:12–27
context: 2 Chronicles 18:12–27 parallels 1 Kings 22:13–28. Micaiah vows, “As the LORD lives, I will say what my God says” (18:13), where Kings has “what the LORD says to me, that I will speak”. He first echoes the other prophets, then describes Israel scattered like sheep without a shepherd and a vision of the LORD’s heavenly court, in which a spirit offers to be a lying spirit in the mouth of Ahab’s prophets. Zedekiah strikes Micaiah, and Ahab sends him to prison until he returns in peace. On the lying spirit (18:18–22), both traditions affirm that God judges justly, that he is not the author of sin, and that Ahab is warned plainly and remains responsible. Classical Arminian readers generally describe God as permitting and directing an evil already chosen, and Reformed readers generally describe God as ordaining and governing evil agents for a just judgment. That difference is already treated at Judges 9:23 and in the notes on 1 Kings 22:19–23, so no new box is added here.

verses.text: The messenger who went to call Micaiah spoke to him, saying, “Behold, the words of the prophets declare good to the king with one mouth. Let your word therefore, please be like one of theirs, and speak good.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The messenger sent to call Micaiah tells him that the prophets declare good to the king with one mouth and urges him to speak good like them. The pressure to conform reaches the prophet himself.

Arminian readers note that the messenger may mean well but asks Micaiah to choose agreement over faithfulness, a temptation that tests the prophet’s free and costly loyalty.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the temptation every messenger of God faces, to soften the word for a favorable hearing, and they note that the true prophet’s message is not his to adjust.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: faithfulness to God’s word can cost a person approval and safety, consistent with the notes on 1 Kings 22:13.

verses.text: Micaiah said, “As the LORD lives, I will say what my God says.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Micaiah answers, “As the LORD lives, I will say what my God says.” Kings has “what the LORD says to me, that I will speak”.

Arminian readers note the prophet’s resolve to be faithful whatever the cost, and they see in his oath a free commitment to speak only what God gives, which sets the standard for the rest of the scene.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers echo this and see in Micaiah’s vow the calling of every true prophet (compare Numbers 22:38), and they note the personal note in Chronicles’ wording, my God, which ties the prophet’s loyalty to his relationship with the LORD.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: God’s servants speak what he gives, not what pleases.

verses.text: When he had come to the king, the king said to him, “Micaiah, shall we go to Ramoth Gilead to battle, or shall I forbear?” He said, “Go up, and prosper. They shall be delivered into your hand.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Asked whether to go to Ramoth Gilead, Micaiah first answers, “Go up, and prosper. They shall be delivered into your hand.” Kings has “the LORD will deliver it into the hand of the king” at this point.

Arminian readers usually read this as irony, since the king immediately suspects he is not hearing the truth.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise usually read the reply as echoing the four hundred in a way the king recognizes as mocking, while noting that the text does not describe Micaiah’s tone, so the irony is inferred from the response.

Both traditions agree, as in the notes on 1 Kings 22:15, that the following verses give Micaiah’s true message, so his first answer is not his final word.

verses.text: The king said to him, “How many times shall I adjure you that you speak to me nothing but the truth in the LORD’s name?”
verses.arminianNotes:
The king asks how many times he must adjure Micaiah to speak nothing but the truth in the LORD’s name. He demands the truth he has already said he hates.

Arminian readers note the irony and see a king who knows the difference between flattery and truth, which makes his later refusal a responsible choice rather than ignorance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a king who recognizes the truth but will not submit to it, and they note that the demand exposes the condition of Ahab’s heart rather than any uncertainty about what the LORD had said.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground, consistent with the notes on 1 Kings 22:16: knowing what is true and obeying it are not the same thing.

verses.text: He said, “I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd. The LORD said, ‘These have no master. Let them each return to his house in peace.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
Micaiah says, “I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd”, and reports the LORD’s word that they have no master and should each return home in peace. The image foretells the king’s death.

Arminian readers note that the word announces judgment while still showing concern for the people.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s word announcing the fall of Israel’s king while showing concern for the people, and they note that the phrase recalls Moses’ prayer for a leader (Numbers 27:17).

Both traditions note that Jesus uses similar language of the crowds (Matthew 9:36), and both read the verse as pastoral as well as a warning.

verses.text: The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “Didn’t I tell you that he would not prophesy good concerning me, but evil?”
verses.arminianNotes:
The king of Israel says to Jehoshaphat, “Didn’t I tell you that he would not prophesy good concerning me, but evil?” The wording matches Kings.

Arminian readers note that Ahab treats the warning as personal hostility rather than a call to change course, and they see him hearing the word only to confirm his prejudice, a choice that leaves him responsible.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a hardened heart that turns a warning into a grievance, and they note that the king’s response confirms what he said about Micaiah in 18:7.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground, consistent with the notes on 1 Kings 22:18: a person can hear God’s word clearly and still refuse it.

verses.text: Micaiah said, “Therefore hear the LORD’s word: I saw the LORD sitting on his throne, and all the army of heaven standing on his right hand and on his left.
verses.arminianNotes:
Micaiah says, “Therefore hear the LORD’s word: I saw the LORD sitting on his throne, and all the army of heaven standing on his right hand and on his left.” Kings has “standing by him on his right hand”.

Arminian readers note that the vision places the earthly kings’ thrones under the LORD’s rule.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see God’s sovereign rule pictured as a king in council, comparable to scenes such as Isaiah 6:1 and Job 1:6. The vision is a prophetic disclosure, and both traditions are cautious about pressing its details.

Both traditions treat the vision as shared ground: what happens at Ramoth Gilead is decided under the LORD’s throne, not at the gate of Samaria.

verses.text: The LORD said, ‘Who will entice Ahab king of Israel, that he may go up and fall at Ramoth Gilead?’ One spoke saying in this way, and another saying in that way.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD asks who will entice Ahab king of Israel, that he may go up and fall at Ramoth Gilead, and different answers are given. Chronicles adds the title king of Israel.

Arminian readers read this as God’s judicial sentence on a king who has repeatedly refused his word, permitting and directing evil already chosen, as discussed at Judges 9:23 and in the notes on 1 Kings 22:20.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God ordaining Ahab’s fall and governing the agents through whom it comes, while Ahab remains responsible for his choice, as discussed at Judges 9:23 and in the notes on 1 Kings 22:20.

Both traditions affirm that God is just, that the judgment is deserved, and that this difference is already covered by the existing Judges 9:23 box.

verses.text: A spirit came out, stood before the LORD, and said, ‘I will entice him.’ “The LORD said to him, ‘How?’
verses.arminianNotes:
A spirit comes out, stands before the LORD, and says, “I will entice him.” The LORD asks how.

Arminian readers usually stress that the evil comes from the spirit’s own willingness, which God permits and uses as a means of judgment on a king who has chosen falsehood, and they note that the spirit’s identity is not stated.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that even this spirit acts only within God’s governing will and for his just purpose, and they likewise note that interpreters differ on the spirit’s identity.

Both traditions agree, as the notes on 1 Kings 22:21 say, that the text does not make God the author of the lie, and they point to Judges 9:23 for the difference in how they describe God’s role.

verses.text: “He said, ‘I will go, and will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.’ “He said, ‘You will entice him, and will prevail also. Go and do so.’
verses.arminianNotes:
The spirit says he will go and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all Ahab’s prophets, and the LORD says that he will entice him and prevail, and tells him to go and do so.

Arminian readers read this as God giving Ahab over to the falsehood he preferred, permitting and directing an evil already chosen, and they stress that God cannot lie (Numbers 23:19).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers read the commission as God ordaining and governing an evil agent to accomplish a just judgment (compare Ezekiel 14:9; 2 Thessalonians 2:11), without himself doing evil.

Both traditions affirm that God tempts no one (James 1:13) and that the guilt remains with those who chose deception; the difference is treated at Judges 9:23 and in the notes on 1 Kings 22:22.

verses.text: “Now therefore, behold, the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouth of these your prophets; and the LORD has spoken evil concerning you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Micaiah concludes, “Now therefore, behold, the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouth of these your prophets; and the LORD has spoken evil concerning you.” Kings has “all these your prophets”.

Arminian readers note that Micaiah tells Ahab exactly what is happening, giving him a real opportunity to turn back before the judgment falls.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note that the deception is unmasked, so that God’s sovereign judgment does not hide the truth from Ahab, and they see the disclosure as part of God’s justice.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: Ahab hears the truth plainly and is responsible for rejecting it, as discussed at Judges 9:23 and in the notes on 1 Kings 22:23.

verses.text: Then Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah came near, and struck Micaiah on the cheek, and said, “Which way did the LORD’s Spirit go from me to speak to you?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Zedekiah son of Chenaanah comes near, strikes Micaiah on the cheek, and asks, “Which way did the LORD’s Spirit go from me to speak to you?” The false prophet answers truth with violence.

Arminian readers note that his question claims the Spirit for himself, and they see a claim to the Spirit that must be tested by its fruit and fulfillment rather than accepted because it is spoken forcefully.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the hostility that God’s faithful messengers often face (compare Jeremiah 20:2), and they note that Micaiah does not strike back.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground, consistent with the notes on 1 Kings 22:24: a claim to the Spirit is tested by its fruit and its fulfillment, not by force.

verses.text: Micaiah said, “Behold, you shall see on that day, when you go into an inner room to hide yourself.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Micaiah says, “Behold, you shall see on that day, when you go into an inner room to hide yourself.” The outcome will reveal who spoke for the LORD.

Arminian readers note that Micaiah leaves the matter to be proved by events, and they observe that the text does not record Zedekiah’s fate, so they avoid adding details to the story.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see Micaiah leaving vindication to God rather than retaliating, and they see in his answer the confidence of a prophet who knows the LORD will confirm his word in his own time.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the true prophet trusts the LORD to confirm his word, consistent with the notes on 1 Kings 22:25.

verses.text: The king of Israel said, “Take Micaiah, and carry him back to Amon the governor of the city, and to Joash the king’s son;
verses.arminianNotes:
The king of Israel orders Micaiah taken back to Amon the governor of the city and to Joash the king’s son. Ahab silences the messenger instead of heeding the message.

Arminian readers note that power is used to suppress an unwelcome word, and they see the king choosing to remove the prophet rather than to reconsider his own course while there is still time.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the pattern of prophets suffering for faithfulness (compare Matthew 5:12), and they note that imprisoning a messenger does not change what God has said.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground, consistent with the notes on 1 Kings 22:26, and read the verse soberly as an injustice suffered by a faithful prophet.

verses.text: and say, ‘The king says, “Put this fellow in the prison, and feed him with bread of affliction and with water of affliction, until I return in peace.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
The king commands that Micaiah be put in prison and fed with bread and water of affliction until he returns in peace. Kings has “until I come in peace” at this point.

Arminian readers note Ahab’s confidence that he will return, and they see his words as setting up a public test of Micaiah’s prophecy, which the king chooses to defy.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see Ahab’s defiance as rejecting the word that warned him, and they note that the king’s own words will be answered by Micaiah’s reply in the next verse.

Both traditions note that Micaiah’s suffering is real, and that the narrative honors his faithfulness under it, consistent with the notes on 1 Kings 22:27.

verses.text: Micaiah said, “If you return at all in peace, the LORD has not spoken by me.” He said, “Listen, you people, all of you!”
verses.arminianNotes:
Micaiah says, “If you return at all in peace, the LORD has not spoken by me”, and adds, “Listen, you people, all of you!” Kings has “Listen, all you people!”

Arminian readers note that he stakes his credibility on the outcome, as Deuteronomy 18:22 directs, and that he calls the people as witnesses to the word.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the prophet’s confidence that the LORD’s word will be fulfilled, and they note that the test is public, so the outcome will vindicate the LORD rather than Micaiah’s own reputation.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: history will vindicate the true word, and the reader will see it happen in the next verses.
